newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Yeltsin, seeking economic answers, meets ministers.
newsitem.headline: Yeltsin, seeking economic answers, meets ministers.

text.p: President Boris Yeltsin, looking for details on how Russia will tackle a raft of economic problems, met his three most senior ministers on Wednesday, the day before planned protests against massive wage arrears.
A Kremlin spokesman said the meeting between Yeltsin and Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin and First Deputy Prime Ministers Anatoly Chubais and Boris Nemtsov had started at noon (0900 GMT).
Yeltsin brought the two first deputy premiers into his government earlier this month and both have already promised to speed up economic reforms.
But the government will have its work cut out to convince Russians that it can resolve the non-payments crisis which has left millions of workers and pensioners struggling to make ends meet.
Workers are owed over 50 trillion roubles ($8.8 billion) in back wages, of which the state owes 10 trillion and many people have not been paid for months.
Trade unions say up to 20 million people will strike or take part in demonstrations during Thursday's day of protests against the arrears, but others are expected to work normally.
The director of the nickel section of Norilsk Nickel's mining and metallurgical combine said workers were satisfied with a deal reached with management on Tuesday.

"There will be some protests tomorrow, but they will in no way affect output or other activities," Mikhail Steklov said. "Besides, it's minus 30 Celsius (minus 22 Fahrenheit), and who wants to stand out in the cold and yell?"
Chernomyrdin is expected to hand Yeltsin his proposals for the last remaining posts in a lengthy cabinet reshuffle and he will then hold a joint news conference with Chubais and Nemtsov.

Yeltsin demanded drastic changes in the government earlier this month. Returning to active politics after eight months of illness, the 66-year-old Kremlin leader acknowledged that his market reforms were failing to meet people's needs.

In an effort to halt the decline in incomes and free the economy from a web of corruption, organised crime and Soviet-style bureaucracy, he parachuted in his 41-year-old chief-of-staff Chubais to spearhead a new wave of reforms.

Last week, in an apparent effort to break a deadlock between Chubais and the more conservative Chernomyrdin, he also named Nemtsov, 37, a liberal regional governor, as a first deputy prime minister with a brief to crack down on monopolists.

In a public show of concern ahead of the protests, the president on Tuesday ordered the government to do more to end wage delays and to help millions of investors who lost their savings in dubious investment schemes. He announced a fund to help war veterans and pensioners deal with their problems.
"I consider the situation with the mass delays in wage payments unbearable," Yeltsin was quoted as saying by his press secretary Sergei Yastrzhembsky.
Government spokesman Igor Shabdurasulov said on Tuesday that Russia could not immediately pay off its debts, but that it could detail its approach to the problem.
"I wouldn't expect any revolutionary decisions in the next three to five days, two weeks, or even month on issues such as natural monopolies, social issues or other problems," he told reporters.
